query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor fraction (around 5–10 at%) of a hexagonal close-packed (HCP) forming element (e.g., Ti or Zr) to the equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW will lower the dislocation core energy and promote alternative slip systems. This modification is expected to enhance room-temperature ductility and improve irradiation tolerance while largely preserving the alloy’s high-temperature mechanical strength and BCC phase stability.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW with excellent high-temperature performance but poor room-temperature ductility and uncertain irradiation resistance.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 5–10 at% of an HCP-forming element (such as Ti or Zr) into NbMoTaW, maintaining an overall BCC-dominated structure.
generation.conditions: Room temperature mechanical tests (e.g., tensile testing), high-temperature mechanical testing up to 1600 °C, and irradiation experiments under helium implantation conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and altered dislocation core characteristics induced by the HCP-forming additive result in regions with modified slip behavior that coexist with the BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The incorporation of an HCP-forming element is hypothesized to lower dislocation core energies and activate additional slip systems, thereby enhancing ductility at room temperature. Simultaneously, the local compositional inhomogeneity may promote defect recombination or trap irradiation-induced defects, mitigating issues such as blistering and amorphization, all while the BCC majority phase upholds high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated NbMoTaW, the doped alloy is predicted to exhibit significantly improved room-temperature ductility (higher plastic strain before fracture) and better irradiation resistance (reduced blistering and defect accumulation), with minimal compromise (ideally <5% reduction) in high-temperature strength and stability up to 1600 °C.
generation.baseline: Untreated, equal-atomic BCC NbMoTaW that performs well at high temperatures but is brittle at room temperature and has not been extensively validated under irradiation.
generation.boundary: The improvements are expected under conditions of room-temperature mechanical loading and radiation environments typical of helium implantation; high-temperature performance (up to approximately 1600 °C) should remain largely unaffected.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the enhanced ductility and irradiation resistance as well as any potential trade-offs, particularly any slight compromises in high-temperature creep behavior, require experimental quantification. The optimum additive concentration and its long‐term phase stability under service conditions also remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of alloys: one consisting of the standard equal-atomic BCC NbMoTaW, and a second where 5–10 at% of a selected HCP-forming element (e.g., Ti) is incorporated while preserving overall BCC structure. Perform room temperature tensile tests to assess ductility, high-temperature (up to 1600 °C) compression or tensile tests to evaluate mechanical strength, and controlled helium implantation experiments to measure irradiation-induced defects and blistering. Microstructural analysis should be conducted using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify phase stability and detect local lattice distortions.
measurements: Room temperature tensile elongation and fracture strain
Yield strength and creep resistance at high temperatures (up to 1600 °C)
Irradiation-induced defect density, blister formation, and possible amorphization metrics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HCP-element-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in room-temperature ductility and reduction in irradiation-induced defects (or if irradiation-induced degradation is equal or worse) without a substantial decrease (>5%) in high-temperature mechanical strength compared with the baseline NbMoTaW, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Intrinsic factors responsible for brittle versus ductile nature of refractory high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are of interest for ultrahigh-temperature applications. To overcome their drawbacks — low-temperature brittleness and poor creep strength at high temperatures — improved fundamental understanding is needed. Using experiments, theory, and modeling, we investigated prototypical body-centered cubic (BCC) RHEAs, TiZrHfNbTa and VNbMoTaW. The former is compressible to 77 K, whereas the latter is not below 298 K. Hexagonal close-packed (HCP) elements in TiZrHfNbTa lower its dislocation core energy, increase lattice distortion, and lower its shear modulus relative to VNbMoTaW whose elements are all BCC. Screw dislocations dominate TiZrHfNbTa plasticity, but equal numbers of edges and screws exist in VNbTaMoW. Dislocation cores are compact in VNbTaMoW and extended in TiZrHfNbTa, and different macroscopic slip planes are activated in the two RHEAs, which we attribute to the concentration of HCP elements. Our findings demonstrate how ductility and strength can be controlled through the ratio of HCP to BCC elements in RHEAs.Subject terms: M
